subject: Cooking
title: Butter vs. Ghee: What Clarifying Does
description: A short lesson to help you apply Butter vs. Ghee: What Clarifying Does.

hook.text: Butter burns at 350°F. Ghee survives past 480°F. Same source, completely different behavior.

buildup.text: Butter is about 80% fat, 15% water, and 5% milk solids. Those solids are what scorch.

discovery.text: Clarifying butter removes water and milk solids, leaving pure butterfat — that's ghee.

twist.text: Indian cooks discovered this thousands of years ago — ghee was essential in tropical climates.

climax.text: Without milk solids, ghee also stays shelf-stable for months without refrigeration.

punchline.text: Ghee is butter that survived purification.

quiz.question: What gives ghee a higher smoke point than butter?
options: Removal of milk solids and water

details.summary: Clarifying butter removes water and milk solids by gently heating until they separate. The remaining pure butterfat — ghee — has a smoke point of 485°F compared to butter's 350°F and lasts months without refrigeration.
details.whyItMatters: Ghee demonstrates how removing water and proteins from butter transforms its cooking properties. The higher smoke point and longer shelf life make it more versatile than regular butter.
takeaways: Clarifying removes water and milk solids from butterfat
Ghee's smoke point reaches 485°F versus butter's 350°F
Pure butterfat resists spoilage for months at room temperature

faq.question: Can people with lactose intolerance eat ghee?
faq.answer: Most lactose-intolerant people tolerate ghee well because clarifying removes nearly all lactose along with the milk solids. The trace amounts remaining are often below the threshold for symptoms. However, those with severe dairy allergies should consult a doctor.

faq.question: What is the difference between ghee and clarified butter?
faq.answer: Clarified butter is heated just enough to separate the components. Ghee is cooked longer until the milk solids brown, adding a nutty, toasted flavor before straining. Both are pure butterfat, but ghee has deeper flavor from the browned solids.
